title: In 2021 an Icelandic peninsula erupted for the first time in about 800 years
body: Iceland’s Reykjanes Peninsula last erupted in the Reykjanes Fires, which ended in 1240. Then, after three weeks in which seismographs recorded more than 40,000 tremors, lava broke through at Fagradalsfjall on 19 March 2021, the peninsula’s first known eruption in about 800 years; the mountain itself had been dormant for some 6,000 years. The magma may have risen through a channel about 17 km long linked to Earth’s mantle, and new eruptions followed in August 2022 and July 2023, each heralded by a swarm of more than 10,000 earthquakes.

cover.alt: Seen from a drone, an oval crater brimming with glowing orange lava on a dark lava field, steam drifting past

slides.alt: Drone view over an oval volcanic crater filled to the brim with molten lava: bright yellow fountains and surges churn across the glowing surface while steam and fumes drift over the black lava field around it.
slides.caption: A drone hovers over the crater of the July 2023 eruption beside Litli-Hrútur, the third eruption in three years: lava boils and surges inside the new cone.

events.text: The Reykjanes Fires, the last eruptions for centuries, end
Lava at Fagradalsfjall, from 19 March to 18 September
A new fissure opens and erupts from 3 to 21 August
Lava breaks out near Litli-Hrútur, 10 July to 5 August

slides.heading: Earthquakes recorded before each eruption
slides.note: At least this many; for 2021, in the last three weeks before the eruption

slides.label: depth of a large magma reservoir under the peninsula
slides.text: It sits at the Moho, the boundary between Earth’s crust and the mantle beneath it. As the 2021 eruption went on, its lava came from ever greater depths.

slides.question: Before 2021, how long had Fagradalsfjall itself been dormant?
slides.explanation: The mountain had been dormant for about 6,000 years, and the whole Reykjanes Peninsula had not erupted for about 800 years.
